##### There are more than 30 Linux signals that can be generated by the system and applications.

| **Signal** | **Value** | **Description**                                    |
| ---------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| SIGHUP     | 1         | Hangs up the process                               |
| SIGINT     | 2         | Interrupts the process                             |
| SIGQUIT    | 3         | Stops the process                                  |
| SIGKILL    | 9         | Unconditionally terminates the process             |
| SIGTERM    | 15        | Terminates the process if possible                 |
| SIGSTOP    | 17        | Unconditionally stops, but doesn't terminate       |
| SIGTSTP    | 18        | Stops or pauses the process, but doesn't terminate |
| SIGCONT    | 19        | Continues a stopped process                        |

Interactive Bash Shell:
SIGINT (Ctrl+C): Bash will stop the current process.
SIGQUIT: If not explicitly handled, Bash can quit (with a core dump).
SIGHUP: It will exit if the terminal is closed or the parent process dies.
SIGTERM: Bash will ignore it unless handled by the user.

### Trapping signals(trapCommand.sh)
##### The trap command in bash allows you to catch and handle specific signals in your script. Instead of the shell processing the signal, your script can take control and decide what to do with it.

##### The format of the trap command is:
###### trap <commands that will get printed> signals.

##### To remove a set trap. Simply add two dashes (Both the single and double dash work properly) after the trap command and a list of the signals you want to return to default behavior.

### Running in the background(background.sh)
##### ampersand symbol after a command, it separates the command from the bash shell and runs it as a separate background process on the system.
###### [1] 3231

##### The number in the square brackets is the job number assigned by the shell to the back ground process. The next number is the Process ID (PID) the Linux system assigns to the process.

##### When the background process fi nishes, it displays a message on the terminal:
###### [1]   Done                    ./test4.sh

##### Be aware that while the background process is running, it still uses your terminal monitor for STDOUT and STDERR messages.

### Running Scripts without a Hang-Up
##### nohup stands for "no hang up",command that allows user to run a command or script in the background even after user log out or close the terminal session.
##### Using nohup, it disassociates the process from the terminal, which means that the process is no longer tied to the terminal's STDOUT (standard output) and STDERR (standard error). Since the terminal session is no longer available to display output or handle errors, nohup redirects the output (both STDOUT and STDERR) to a file called **nohup.out** by default.
###### If user run another command using nohup, the output is appended to the existing nohup.out file.

### Controlling the Job(jobcontrolling.sh)
###### The function of starting, stopping, killing, and resuming jobs is called job control.
###### $$ variable to display the PID that the Linux system assigns to the script.
| **Parameter** | **Description**                                                                                |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-l`          | Lists the **PID** of the process along with the **job number**.                                |
| `-n`          | Lists only jobs that have **changed their status** since the last notification from the shell. |
| `-p`          | Lists only the **PIDs** of the jobs.                                                           |
| `-r`          | Lists only the **running jobs**.                                                               |
| `-s`          | Lists only **stopped jobs**.                                                                   |

###### The job with the plus sign is considered the default job.
###### The job with the minus sign is the job that would become the default job when the current default job fi nishes processing.
###### There will be only one job with the plus sign and one job with the minus sign at any time
###### [1]   1950 Running                 ./test10.sh > test10a.out
###### [2]-  1952 Running                 ./test10.sh > test10b.out 
###### [3]+  1955 Running                 ./test10.sh > test10c.out

###### The + sign indicates the "current" job or the last job that was foregrounded.

### Scheduling a job using the at command
###### The at command in Linux allows users to schedule one-time tasks that will be executed at a specific time in the future.
###### The basic at command format is pretty simple: 
###### at [-f filename] time
###### To handle output that would normally be displayed on the terminal (i.e., STDOUT and STDERR), Linux sends the output via email to the user who submitted the job. This is the default behavior.

##### Listing pending jobs
###### The atq command allows you to view what jobs are pending on the system

##### Removing jobs
###### Use atrm command to remove a pending job

### Starting scripts with a new shell
###### When a user starts a new bash shell session, certain startup files are run automatically, depending on the type of shell session (interactive login shell or non-login shell). This allows you to configure the environment for that session, set shell features, or execute specific scripts.
